## ARTICLE INFO ABSTRACT

### _Keywords:_ Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping language education, making AI literacy crucial for teachers to engage 

AI literacy critically and effectively with this technology. Nonetheless, most existing assessments target students or general Language teacher education users, leaving a gap in measuring AI literacy within language teacher education. This study sought to develop Psychometric properties

and validate the Teachers' AI Literacy Scale (TAILS), grounded in the ED-AI literacy framework, which comprises 

Instrument development

six dimensions: knowledge, evaluation, collaboration, contextualization, autonomy, and ethics. The scale was 

Instrument validation

tested with preservice English language teachers through two phases: exploratory factor analysis (EFA) with 165 participants and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) with a separate sample of 227. Results confirmed a six-factor structure with high internal consistency (Cronbach's α values _\>_ 0.90) and acceptable model fit indices (Chi- square/df = 1.766, RMSEA = 0.058, SRMR = 0.054, TLI = 0.908, CFI = 0.919), demonstrating strong validity and reliability. Each dimension aligned clearly with the competencies required for AI-integrated language teaching. The TAILS is a psychometrically robust, context-specific instrument for assessing AI literacy in lan- guage teacher education. This study bridges the gap between theoretical frameworks and practical assessment, offering a foundation for curriculum development, professional training, and policymaking. Its application supports the preparation of AI-competent educators equipped to navigate the ethical, pedagogical, and tech-

nological demands of the digital classroom.

As facilitators of communicative practice rather than mere users of tech- nology, language teachers must evaluate AI-generated language output, mediate its pedagogical appropriateness for specific learners and con- texts, and balance automation with human interaction ([Chiu et al., 2024;](#appendix-2-content-validity-index-and-modified-kappa) [Chu et al., 2023)](#appendix-2-content-validity-index-and-modified-kappa). These responsibilities call for a discipline-specific AI literacy profile that foregrounds pedagogical agency, contextual adaptation, collaborative orchestration, and ethical decision-making. Such dimensions extend beyond the scope of generic AI literacy constructs and underscore the need for a specialized assess- ment framework in language teacher education.

Although existing research underscores the significance of AI literacy in enhancing pedagogical practices and enriching student learning ex- periences ([Boscardin et al., 2023;](#appendix-2-content-validity-index-and-modified-kappa) Ibrahim, 2024), multiple AI literacy frameworks and instruments have primarily been developed for stu- dents, nonexperts, or general users. For instance, the Artificial Intelli- gence Literacy Questionnaire (AILQ) assesses affective, behavioral, cognitive, and ethical dimensions (Ng et al., 2023), while the AI Literacy Scale (AILS) focuses on awareness, usage, evaluation, and ethics (Wang et al., 2022). Other instruments, such as the Meta AILS (MAILS), AI Anxiety Scale (AIAS), and nonexpert-focused frameworks ([Carolus et al., 2023;](#appendix-2-content-validity-index-and-modified-kappa) Laupichler et al., 2023; Wang & Wang, 2022), similarly privilege general technological engagement or psychological responses to AI. Conceptually, these instruments fall short in capturing teachers’ peda- gogical agency, contextual decision-making, and professional auton- omy; practically, they risk reducing AI literacy to generic competencies that fail to inform instructional design, ethical classroom use, or teacher professional development. As a result, the absence of a discipline-sensitive assessment framework obscures how language teachers interpret, adapt, and govern AI use within instructional contexts.

This shortcoming constitutes a clear theoretical gap (Lim, 2026). While AI literacy is widely acknowledged as essential, existing schol- arship inadequately theorizes how AI literacy manifests as a professional competence in language teacher education, and how it differs from learner- or user-oriented conceptions. When this gap is left unaddressed, AI literacy remains under-specified as a construct, limiting both theo- retical advancement and practical applicability. Teachers may be eval- uated using instruments that are misaligned with their instructional realities, leading to weak construct validity, superficial professional insights, and poorly targeted teacher education interventions. While prior studies have emphasized the role of AI in optimizing language learning ([Gyawali & Mehandroo, 2022)](#appendix-2-content-validity-index-and-modified-kappa), limited empirical work has systematically examined AI literacy as a multidimensional, pedagogically grounded construct among language teachers themselves. This lack of theory-informed measurement hinders the field's ability to assess teachers' preparedness, compare competency profiles, or examine how AI literacy relates to instructional decision-making and ethical practice. In theoretical terms, the problem lies not merely in the absence of an instrument, but in the absence of a construct specification that reflects teachers' situated roles as designers, evaluators, collaborators, and ethical agents in AI-mediated language education.

To address this gap, the present study develops and validates the Teachers’ AI Literacy Scale (TAILS) for language teacher education. Grounded in the ED-AI literacy framework ([Allen & Kendeou, 2024)](#appendix-2-content-validity-index-and-modified-kappa), TAILS conceptualizes AI literacy across six theoretically distinct yet interrelated dimensions: knowledge, evaluation, collaboration, contex- tualization, autonomy, and ethics. Theoretically, this study contributes by adapting and extending AI literacy theory to a discipline-specific professional context, thereby advancing construct clarity and contex- tualized theorization (Lim, 2026). This represents an incremental yet meaningful theoretical extension, as it shifts AI literacy from a gener- alized competence model toward a profession- and pedagogy-sensitive framework that foregrounds teacher agency and ethical responsibility.

The theoretical interestingness of this study lies in its reframing of AI literacy as a pedagogical and ethical capacity rather than a purely technical one, contextualized in language teacher education. By sys- tematically operationalizing this reconceptualization through psycho- metric validation, the study bridges theory development and empirical testing. Practically, the validated TAILS instrument enables language educators, teacher education programs, and policymakers to diagnose AI literacy competencies, design targeted professional development, and guide responsible AI integration in language education.

## 2. Literature review

### _2.1._ _Defining AI literacy_

AI literacy refers to the ability to understand, utilize, evaluate, and critically analyze AI technologies and their impacts, allowing in- dividuals to effectively interact with AI systems and apply them across multiple contexts ([Chiu et al., 2024)](#appendix-2-content-validity-index-and-modified-kappa). Core components of AI literacy include the capacity to critically assess AI technologies, communicate with AI systems, and collaborate effectively in environments where AI plays a significant role ([Fan & Zhang, 2024;](#appendix-2-content-validity-index-and-modified-kappa) Ng et al., 2021). Despite general agreement on its importance, definitions and frameworks typi- cally overlap, highlighting the need for a diverse yet cohesive educa- tional approach to AI (Otero et al., 2023). Additionally, some studies advocate for integrating AI literacy into existing curricula at all educa- tional levels—from early childhood and K–12 to higher education—to foster a more comprehensive development of AI competencies (Otero et al., 2023; Relmasira et al., 2023; Yetis¸ensoy & Rapoport, 2023). The call for educators to optimize their AI literacy is increasingly urgent. As stewards of AI literacy, educators must be equipped to effectively guide students in navigating the complexities of AI ([Boscardin et al., 2023;](#appendix-2-content-validity-index-and-modified-kappa) Ibrahim, 2024). Numerous studies emphasize the significance of teacher preparedness, recommending targeted training and curriculum development to ensure educators possess the necessary skills to effectively integrate AI tools into their teaching practices (Yeter et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2022). Programs aimed at developing AI literacy must strike a balance between technical profi- ciency and ethical awareness. Students need to learn not only how to utilize AI tools but also how to critically evaluate their broader societal implications ([Biagini, 2024;](#appendix-2-content-validity-index-and-modified-kappa) [Choi et al., 2024)](#appendix-2-content-validity-index-and-modified-kappa). This balanced approach seeks to cultivate responsible AI users who are aware of the ethical di- mensions and long-term consequences of their engagement with AI technologies.

In the context of English language education, AI literacy involves the knowledge and ability to effectively engage with AI technologies that influence language learning and teaching practices. Research highlights that AI can significantly refine the quality of English language acquisi- tion by promoting personalized learning experiences ([Gyawali & Mehandroo, 2022)](#appendix-2-content-validity-index-and-modified-kappa). Developing AI literacy goes beyond understanding how AI tools function; it also requires the cultivation of critical digital skills to navigate these technologies effectively. Recent studies under- score the importance of critical digital literacy—particularly in relation to AI—as it encourages learners to engage with AI tools analytically, strengthening their cognitive development and critical thinking skills (Joseph, 2023; Wang et al., 2024). This competency is particularly crucial as learners increasingly interact with advanced applications, such as ChatGPT, which can significantly shape their learning processes (Joseph, 2023; Wei, 2023).

Furthermore, AI literacy fosters a deeper understanding of the ethical considerations surrounding the use of AI in education. As AI technolo- gies become more integrated into language learning environments, concerns have emerged regarding inclusivity, fairness, and the ethical implications of relying on automated systems ([AlAfnan, 2024)](#appendix-2-content-validity-index-and-modified-kappa). Thus, knowledge about AI must transcend technical skills and include an awareness of its cultural and societal impacts ([AlAfnan, 2024)](#appendix-2-content-validity-index-and-modified-kappa). This broader perspective allows both educators and learners to critically

Quantitatively, the Content Validity Index (CVI) was used to oper-

reliability.

ationalize expert judgments. At the item level, the item-level CVI (I-CVI) was determined by calculating the proportion of experts who rated a quality indicator's relevance as three or higher on a 4-point Likert scale 

(1 = totally irrelevant, 2 = irrelevant, 3 = relevant, and 4 = totally relevant). At the dimension level, the scale-level CVI (S-CVI) was computed as the average of the I-CVI scores across all items within a given dimension. According to Polit et al. (2007), a scale is considered to have excellent content validity when each item attains an I-CVI of at least 0.78 and the scale-level content validity index/averaging method (S-CVI/Ave) reaches 0.90 or higher. The scale-level content validity index and universal agreement (S-CVI/UA) were calculated. Addition- ally, the modified kappa (κ\*) was employed to adjust for potential chance agreement among experts, with values of at least 0.75 indicating acceptable levels of agreement (Polit et al., 2007).

Qualitatively, experts provided written feedback addressing termi- nological appropriateness, linguistic clarity, conceptual alignment with the ED-AI literacy framework, and potential ambiguities in item phrasing. This qualitative feedback served a complementary function to the CVI statistics by identifying areas where items could be improved for clarity and interpretability without altering their conceptual intent. The integration of quantitative CVI indices and qualitative expert commen- tary ensured that the instrument was both conceptually representative and clearly articulated, thereby strengthening its substantive foundation prior to pilot testing and subsequent psychometric validation.

##### _3.1.1.3._ _Step 3: Pilot study for face validity._ To further evaluate the 

suitability and usability of the scale, a pilot study was conducted to establish face validity as an early-stage form of validity evidence focused on participants’ intuitive understanding of the instrument. Face validity refers to the extent to which a measure appears, on the surface, to assess the intended construct, as judged by nonexperts such as test-takers. It focuses on aspects such as feasibility, readability, style consistency, and clarity of language (Taherdoost, 2016). The pilot study involved 30 preservice English language teachers in Indonesia, a sample size that is appropriate for face validity assessment and justified by the principle of data saturation, whereby additional participants no longer yield sub- stantively new feedback regarding item clarity, comprehensibility, or relevance (Lim, 2024). During the pilot phase, no substantively new concerns emerged after successive rounds of participant feedback, indicating that saturation had been reached. In addition, response time and ease of completion were assessed to ensure operational feasibility. Although participants reported no major difficulties in understanding or responding to the items, they provided minor suggestions aimed at improving wording precision and stylistic consistency, which were incorporated into the revised instrument.

#### _3.1.2._ _Phase II: Validation of the scale (psychometric property testing)_

##### _3.1.2.1._ _Step 4: Construct validity._ Construct validity was rigorously 

assessed through a two-stage factor-analytic approach, comprising exploratory factor analysis (EFA) followed by confirmatory factor analysis (CFA). In the initial step, EFA was conducted using principal component analysis (PCA) with varimax rotation. PCA was selected at this stage as a data-reduction technique appropriate for early-scale development, where the primary objective was to explore the dimen- sional structure and identify a parsimonious factor solution (Yusoff et al., 2021). To ensure the data's suitability for EFA, the Kai- ser–Meyer–Olkin (KMO) measure and Bartlett's test of sphericity were conducted, verifying the adequacy of the sample and the correlation between variables. The number of factors retained was determined on the basis of multiple criteria, encompassing eigenvalues, scree plot in- spection, factor loadings, and the percentage of explained variance (Yusoff et al., 2021). These criteria were crucial for identifying a meaningful and robust factor structure, ensuring that the instrument's dimensions were properly represented. Additionally, a robustness check was conducted. Specifically, the EFA was re-estimated using a principal axis factoring with promax rotation, which allows factors to correlate and is theoretically consistent with the multidimensional nature of AI 

literacy. Following EFA, the factor structure was further validated using CFA. CFA was estimated using covariance-based structural equation modeling within SmartPLS 4. Although SmartPLS is widely recognized for partial least squares estimation, the current analysis employed covariance- based model estimation procedures supported by SmartPLS 4, using maximum likelihood estimation. Model fit evaluation emphasized Comparative Fit Index (CFI) and Tucker–Lewis Index (TLI) values near or above 0.90, alongside Root Mean Square Error of Approximation (RMSEA) values below 0.08. The chi-square to degrees of freedom ratio (χ[^2]/df) was also examined, with values below 5 indicating acceptable fit (Hu & Bentler, 1999; Yusoff et al., 2021). Goodness of Fit Index (GFI) and Adjusted Goodness of Fit Index (AGFI) were treated as supple- mentary diagnostics rather than primary decision rules.

##### _3.1.2.2._ _Step 5: Internal consistency testing._ The internal consistency 

reliability of the instrument was assessed using Cronbach's alpha, with values calculated separately for each factor to ensure that each dimen- sion demonstrated sufficient reliability. Cronbach's alpha is a widely employed statistic for evaluating the degree of consistency within a set of items measuring the same construct. Calculating it separately for each factor enabled us to assess the reliability of each specific dimension. According to Taherdoost (2016), the recommended thresholds for newly developed instruments are as follows: excellent (0.90 and above), high (0.70–0.90), moderate (0.50–0.70), and low (0.50 and below). These benchmarks provide a standard for determining whether the reliability of the instrument falls within an acceptable range. In addition to Cronbach's alpha, we also calculated the composite reliability for each dimension, which offers a more comprehensive measure of internal consistency by considering the relationships among all items within a particular factor.

### _3.2._ _Context and participants_

This research involved preservice English language teachers enrolled in universities offering English language teacher education programs in Indonesia. Participants were selected through convenience sampling, a method chosen for its practicality, cost-effectiveness, and efficiency compared with other sampling techniques. Additionally, eligibility criteria encompassed participants' willingness to take part in the study and prior experience teaching English. This population was considered particularly appropriate for the intended use of the TAILS because pre- service teachers constitute a critical transitional group, simultaneously developing pedagogical knowledge, professional identity, and disposi- tions toward the pedagogically responsible integration of AI technolo- gies. As such, the study's research design, sampling strategy, and validation claims are intentionally bounded to this population and educational context. Consequently, interpretations of the findings and applications of TAILS beyond comparable preservice English language teacher education settings should be made with caution and supported by further validation in alternative populations and contexts. A total of 422 preservice teachers participated in the research, distributed across distinct stages of instrument validation. 30 in- dividuals were involved in the pilot study to refine and assess the clarity of the instrument, 165 participated in EFA to identify the underlying factor structure, and 227 were assessed for CFA to validate the proposed model and confirm the instrument's reliability and validity. Specifically, [Table 3](#33-data-collection-and-ethical-considerations) exhibits the descriptive statistics of the participants: sample 1 (N = 165) for EFA and sample 2 (N = 227) for CFA. In sample 1, most participants were female (77.6%), while males comprised 22.4%. Most participants were aged 18–20 years (62.4%), followed by those aged 21–23 years (33.3%), a small group aged 24–26 years (3.6%), and only one participant aged 27 or older (0.6%). Regarding academic level, most were in their second year (37.0%), followed by the third year (35.8%), fourth year or higher (19.4%), and first year (7.9%). The majority

The third fac- tor—_Collaboration_—contained five items with loadings from 0.442 to 0.600, an eigenvalue of 1.098 contributing 3.659% of the variance, and a Cronbach's alpha of 0.759. The fourth fac- tor—_Contextualization_—consisted of five items with loadings ranging from 0.399 to 0.631, an eigenvalue of 1.355 explaining 4.517% of the variance, and a Cronbach's alpha of 0.851. The fifth fac- tor—_Autonomy_—included five items with loadings between 0.457 and 0.794, a notably high eigenvalue of 11.458, accounting for 38.194% of the variance, and a Cronbach's alpha of 0.829. Although this eigenvalue is substantially larger than those of the other factors, it reflects the central role of autonomy as a foundational competence underlying teachers' engagement with AI in educational contexts. In the context of preservice teacher education, autonomy-related items, such as inde- pendent decision-making, self-directed learning of AI tools, and confi- dence in managing AI use, tend to show strong intercorrelations, which can result in a dominant first-order factor during exploratory analysis. Importantly, this interpretation is supported by the theoretical posi- tioning of autonomy within the ED-AI framework, where agency and self-regulation are conceptualized as enabling conditions for other AI- related competencies. The sixth factor—_Ethics_—also comprised five items, with loadings ranging from 0.596 to 0.794, an eigenvalue of 2.224 explaining 7.412% of the variance, and a Cronbach's alpha of 0.867. Overall, the six-factor model explained 63.965% of the total variance, with each factor demonstrating acceptable to strong internal consistency, as indicated by Cronbach's alpha values ranging from 0.759 to 0.867.

### _4.3._ _Confirmatory factor analysis_

After identifying the factor structure of the TAILS through EFA, we conducted a CFA using the remaining subsample to validate the model. Model fit was assessed utilizing multiple indices, encompassing Chi- square/df, RMSEA, SRMR, TLI, and CFI (see [Table 5)](#43-confirmatory-factor-analysis). The initial CFA,

based on the EFA-derived 30-item model, demonstrated a good fit ac- cording to the Chi-square/df, RMSEA, and SRMR values (Kline, 2016). Nonetheless, the CFI (0.893) and TLI (0.881) approached, but did not fully reach, the recommended 0.90 threshold, indicating potential areas for model refinement.

Model modification decisions were guided by both statistical evi- dence and theoretical considerations rather than fit improvement alone. Examination of standardized factor loadings revealed that two items (CON2 and EVA5) loaded weakly (_\<_0.60) on their intended constructs, suggesting limited contribution to construct representation. Conceptu- ally, item CON2 emphasized general support for students with special needs, which overlapped with the knowledge and autonomy dimensions rather than uniquely capturing contextual adaptation, while item EVA5 focused on fairness in AI-based assessment, a concept more centrally aligned with the ethics dimension. Their removal therefore reduced construct ambiguity and improved conceptual distinctiveness without compromising core content coverage. The revised model yielded a modest improvement in fit (CFI = 0.898; TLI = 0.885). Further in- spection identified one additional item (COL2) with a loading below 0.60, which was removed in the subsequent model. Item COL2 empha- sized general teamwork support rather than explicit human–AI collab- oration, making it less theoretically central to the collaboration construct as defined in the ED-AI framework. Its removal strengthened the construct's focus on pedagogically meaningful AI-mediated collab- oration. Importantly, each affected dimension retained at least four conceptually coherent items, ensuring adequate coverage of the un- derlying construct. Modification indices further indicated substantial shared residual variance between two ethics items (ETH1 and ETH2). Rather than relying solely on statistical criteria, the decision to correlate these error terms was guided by clear theoretical and substantive con- siderations grounded in the content of the items. ETH1 and ETH2 both reflect closely related aspects of ethical responsibility in AI-mediated teaching. Specifically, decisions about selecting AI tools are inherently linked to considerations of data privacy, as teachers must evaluate how AI systems collect, store, and process student data before adopting them for classroom use. From a pedagogical and ethical standpoint, these judgments are often made concurrently within teachers' ethical

### _4.4._ _Reliability_

The internal consistency and reliability of the TAILS were assessed utilizing Cronbach's alpha and composite reliability (CR) for each of its six dimensions. All dimensions demonstrated excellent reliability, with values well above the recommended threshold of 0.70. As shown in [Table 6,](#44-reliability) the _Contextualization_ dimension has the highest reliability, with a Cronbach's alpha of 0.949 and a CR of 0.935. This was followed by the _Ethics_ (α = 0.945, CR = 0.949) and _Collaboration_ (α = 0.925, CR = 0.937) dimensions. The _Evaluation_ and _Knowledge_ dimensions each had a Cronbach's alpha of 0.920, with CRs of 0.925 and 0.941, respectively. Finally, the _Autonomy_ dimension demonstrated a Cronbach's alpha of 0.903 and a CR of 0.940. These findings demonstrate that each dimen- sion of the scale possesses robust internal consistency and composite reliability, reinforcing the robustness of the TAILS as a tool for assessing AI literacy in teacher education.

### _4.5._ _Validity_

To confirm the scale's convergent validity, AVE values were calcu- lated to examine the extent to which items within each construct are correlated. According to [Fornell and Larcker (1981),](#appendix-2-content-validity-index-and-modified-kappa) convergent validity should be examined using three criteria: (1) internal consistency reli- ability (Cronbach's alpha), (2) CR, and (3) AVE. As presented in [Table 6,](#44-reliability) the AVE values for the six dimensions of the TAILS ranged from 0.454 to 0.538, calculated from the standardized factor loadings of the finalized 27-item measurement model. Specifically, _Ethics_ (0.538) and _Contextu-_ _alization_ (0.512) exceeded the commonly recommended threshold of 0.50, indicating that these constructs explain more than half of the variance in their respective indicators. The remaining dimensions—- _Knowledge_ (0.476), _Evaluation_ (0.472), _Collaboration_ (0.473), and _Au-_ _tonomy_ (0.454)—yielded AVE values slightly below the 0.50 benchmark. However, all constructs demonstrated strong CR (all exceeding 0.70, as proposed by Nunnally & Bernstein, 1994) and high Cronbach's alpha values (all above 0.70, as recommended by Hair et al., 2006), suggesting satisfactory internal consistency. Consistent with methodological guid- ance of [Fornell and Larcker (1981),](#appendix-2-content-validity-index-and-modified-kappa) when CR is high, AVE values marginally below 0.50 may still indicate adequate convergent validity. Taken together, these results provide acceptable and theoretically coherent evidence of convergent validity for the TAILS measurement model.

Discriminant validity, which assesses whether items within a construct are more strongly associated with each other than with items from other constructs, was explored utilizing the Heterotrait–Monotrait 

**Table 6** 

Dimensions Cronbach's alpha

ratio of correlations (HTMT), as recommended by Henseler et al. (2015). The results presented in Table 7 confirm that all HTMT values ranged from 0.613 to 0.874, well below the accepted threshold of 0.90 ([Gold et al., 2001)](#appendix-2-content-validity-index-and-modified-kappa), thereby indicating satisfactory discriminant validity. The six dimensions represent related facets of teacher AI literacy, which support interpreting HTMT values below 0.90 as acceptable separation in a multidimensional scale (Lim et al., 2026). One HTMT value approached this benchmark, which signals close proximity between the relevant dimensions and motivates future item refinement and replica- tion checks in new samples. To further strengthen the evidence for discriminant validity, bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals for the HTMT estimates were examined using 1000 resamples. As shown in Table 7, none of the upper bounds of the HTMT confidence intervals exceeded the critical value of 1.00, indicating that all latent constructs are empirically distinct. This result provides additional robustness beyond point estimates alone and reduces concerns regarding potential construct overlap among the six dimensions of the TAILS. Additionally, Pearson correlations were calculated between the six subscales of the finalized 27-item TAILS (N = 227) and two established measures: AI self-efficacy ([Ayanwale et al., 2024;](#appendix-2-content-validity-index-and-modified-kappa) [Carolus et al., 2023)](#appendix-2-content-validity-index-and-modified-kappa) and attitude toward AI questionnaires (Losada et al., 2023; Nordlof, ¨ Hallstrom, ¨ & Host, 2019¨ ; Yue et al., 2024) to assess concurrent criterion validity (see Table 8). While these three scales investigate related but distinct constructs, the TAILS was anticipated to correlate positively with both AI self-efficacy and attitude toward AI. As exhibited in Table 8, all correlations were statistically significant (_p \<_ 0.01). To aid interpretation, correlation magnitudes were evaluated using [Cohen's (1988)](#appendix-2-content-validity-index-and-modified-kappa) effect size guidelines, where coefficients of approximately 0.10 indicate small, 0.30 moderate, and 0.50 or above large associations. The intercorrelations among the six TAILS subscales ranged from 0.530 to 0.695, corresponding to large effect sizes, indicating strong and theo- retically coherent relationships among the dimensions while still reflecting their conceptual distinctiveness. Correlations between each TAILS dimension and AI self-efficacy ranged from 0.476 to 0.661, falling within the moderate-to-large range, while correlations with attitudes toward AI ranged from 0.491 to 0.690, also reflecting moderate-to-large effect sizes. These results offer evidence for the good concurrent crite- rion validity of the TAILS, exhibiting meaningful associations with established measures that assess related yet distinct constructs.

## 5. Discussion

This research sought to develop and validate the TAILS, grounded in the ED-AI literacy framework ([Allen & Kendeou, 2024)](#appendix-2-content-validity-index-and-modified-kappa) and to assess its psychometric properties within the context of English language teacher education. The results provide strong evidence that the TAILS is a reli- able and valid instrument for exploring preservice English language teachers' AI literacy across six key dimensions: _Knowledge_, _Evaluation_, _Collaboration_, _Contextualization_, _Autonomy_, and _Ethics_. The psychometric evaluation—including both exploratory and confirmatory factor analy- ses—revealed a six-factor structure that aligned well with the theoretical framework. All dimensions exhibited high internal consistency (Cron- bach's α _\>_ 0.90) and appropriate model fit indices in the final CFA (CFI = 0.919, TLI = 0.908, RMSEA = 0.058), meeting the psychometric standards recommended by Kline (2016) and Hu and Bentler (1999).

Overall, this work makes several meaningful contributions to the field. It introduces a validated, theory-informed tool for assessing AI literacy specifically in English language teacher education—an area largely underserved by existing generalized tools. Additionally, the research empirically supports the multidimensional nature of AI liter- acy, emphasizing the significance of ethical awareness, contextual adaptability, and collaborative competence for effective AI integration. Moreover, the TAILS instrument holds practical value: it can inform teacher training curricula, guide professional development initiatives, and support educational policy aimed at preparing educators for AI- enhanced classrooms.

### _5.1._ _Strengths, limitations, and future research directions_

One of the key strengths of this study lies in its rigorous methodo- logical approach, particularly the integration of exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, which ensured the robustness and struc- tural validity of TAILS. Grounded in the ED-AI literacy framework ([Allen & Kendeou, 2024)](#appendix-2-content-validity-index-and-modified-kappa), the instrument addresses a notable gap in the liter- ature by providing a psychometrically validated, theory-driven tool specifically tailored to English language teacher education. From an educational perspective, the study advances innovation in language teacher education by operationalizing the ED-AI literacy framework into a practical assessment instrument that reflects the professional and pedagogical realities of language teachers, rather than focusing on stu- dents or general users as in most existing AI literacy measures. This shift represents a move from generic technological competence toward pedagogically grounded AI literacy. Moreover, the multidimensional structure of the TAILS enables data-informed curriculum development and personalized teacher preparation by identifying preservice teachers’ strengths and needs across key dimensions. As such, teacher education programs can design targeted instructional interventions that foster more reflective, responsible, and context-sensitive AI integration, posi- tioning the study as a contribution not only to measurement develop- ment but also to evidence-based and adaptive innovation in AI-enhanced teaching and learning environments.

Despite these strengths, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, data were collected using self-report measures, which may be subject to social desirability bias and respondents' self-perceptions of their AI literacy rather than observed instructional practices. Second, a marker-variable test was not conducted to quantify potential common method variance, which leaves residual uncertainty regarding method- driven covariance in the observed relationships. Third, the study focused exclusively on preservice teachers, which limits the extent to which the findings can be generalized to in-service or experienced lan- guage teachers whose professional responsibilities and exposure to AI tools may differ substantially. Fourth, the sample was drawn from an Indonesian context, and although this provides valuable insight into AI literacy development, the cultural, institutional, and technological conditions of teacher education in Indonesia may differ from those in other regions. As a result, caution is warranted when generalizing the findings to different national or cross-cultural contexts. Fifth, the pilot study involved a relatively small sample, which, although sufficient for establishing face validity and item clarity, limits the generalizability of the pilot findings. The pilot sample size was determined based on saturation, as no substantial new issues regarding item comprehension or clarity emerged; however, given the cross-cultural and context- sensitive nature of AI literacy, a larger and more diverse pilot sample could have provided additional insights. Sixth, the cross-sectional design restricts the ability to examine how teachers’ AI literacy develops over time. Finally, Despite the comprehensive validity evidence presented, some aspects of validity remain untested. Specifically, the study did not examine nomological validity in terms of how TAILS relates to broader 

teacher competency frameworks, nor did it assess predictive validity. Future research should validate TAILS with in-service language teachers and employ longitudinal designs to examine the stability and developmental sensitivity of AI literacy across career stages. Cross- cultural measurement invariance testing across different countries and educational systems is also necessary to support meaningful interna- tional comparisons. Future research should test measurement invariance across key subgroups such as gender, academic level, and teaching experience before comparing scores across groups. Evidence for con- figural, metric, and scalar invariance would support meaningful sub- group comparisons. Future research should also evaluate whether the six dimensions can be modeled as a higher-order teacher artificial intelli- gence literacy construct using hierarchical component modeling, which would clarify whether reporting both dimension scores and an overall score is justified. Incorporating multi-method approaches beyond self- report would further strengthen the instrument's validity and explana- tory power. Finally, future studies are recommended to examine the nomological validity of TAILS by situating it within broader teacher competency frameworks and to establish its predictive validity by investigating its ability to predict teachers' instructional practices and professional outcomes related to AI use.

### _5.2._ _Implications_

The findings of this study have important implications for teacher education, curriculum development, educational policy, and pedagog- ical theory. By providing a validated, context-specific instrument for assessing AI literacy in language teacher education, the TAILS offers teacher educators a practical tool to diagnose preservice teachers' strengths and areas for development across multiple dimensions. Within teacher education programs, the TAILS can inform curriculum design by aligning course objectives, learning activities, and assessments with AI literacy dimensions such as evaluation, contextualization, collaboration, autonomy, and ethics, thereby supporting the systematic integration of pedagogically grounded AI competencies. The scale may be used diag- nostically at program entry and evaluatively following AI-focused coursework to monitor learning gains, guide curriculum refinement, and support targeted professional development. At the program and policy levels, aggregated TAILS data enable data-driven decision-mak- ing for embedding AI literacy within teacher education frameworks and for evaluating trends across cohorts, institutions, or demographic groups. Beyond assessment, the multidimensional data generated by TAILS support educational and pedagogical data analytics, including longitudinal tracking of teachers’ AI literacy development over time. Theoretically, the scale aligns with constructivist and sociocultural learning perspectives by emphasizing critical evaluation, contextualized AI use, collaboration, teacher agency, and ethical responsibility. Collectively, these implications position AI literacy as a pedagogically grounded, reflective, and values-oriented construct, supporting the preparation of adaptive and responsible language educators in AI- enhanced learning environments.

## 6. Conclusion

This research successfully developed and validated TAILS, a comprehensive and reliable instrument grounded in the ED-AI literacy framework, specifically designed for language teacher education. The scale's six-factor structure, which comprises _Knowledge_, _Evaluation_, _Collaboration_, _Contextualization_, _Autonomy_, and _Ethics_, reflects the multifaceted competencies essential for navigating AI-enhanced teach- ing and learning environments. The robust psychometric evidence af- firms its potential for use in both research and practice, offering a valuable tool for assessing preservice teachers' AI literacy and informing teacher training programs. This study addresses a critical gap in existing AI literacy assessments and contributes meaningfully to the advance- ment of teacher preparedness in the age of AI. Future research should

## Appendix 1. The table below exhibits the originally administered 30-item scale. Based on the findings of the CFA, three items (CON2, EVA5, and COL2) were removed, and a pair of items (ETH1 and ETH2) was allowed to correlate. Thus, the final model comprised a refined 27-item version of the TAILS

Teachers' AI Literacy Scale (TAILS)

Codes Items Removal & Correlation based on CFA

**Knowledge (KNO)** KNO1 1. I know that AI can help teachers create personalized learning for students. ​

KNO2 2. I am familiar with some common AI tools that support teaching and learning in classrooms (e.g., ChatGPT). ​ KNO3 3. I know that AI can support students with different learning needs. ​

KNO4 4. I know that AI can assist teachers in lesson planning and material development. ​ KNO5 5. I am aware that AI applications can help teachers with assessment. ​

**Evaluation (EVA)** EVA1 6. I am capable of comparing the effectiveness of different AI tools for classroom use. ​

EVA2 7. I can select the most appropriate solution from different options provided by AI applications. ​ EVA3 8. I can choose the right educational AI tools based on the specific task. ​

EVA4 9. I can evaluate how AI recommendations align with curriculum standards and goals. ​ EVA5 10. I can analyze whether AI assessment tools for students are accurate and fair. Remove **Collaboration (COL)**

COL1 11. I can collaborate with AI tools to design engaging lessons. ​ COL2 12. I can use AI to support teamwork among students in group projects. Remove COL3 13. I can communicate effectively with AI tools to modify group learning activities based on student needs. ​

COL4 14. I feel comfortable integrating feedback from AI systems into collaborative lesson planning. ​ COL5 15. I can facilitate student collaboration using AI-enhanced platforms (e.g., Padlet). ​

**Contextualization (CON)** CON1 16. I can integrate AI tools into lesson plans to enhance specific subjects, such as language learning. ​

CON2 17. I understand how to use AI to support students with specific needs. Remove CON3 18. I can design classroom activities that encourage students to explore AI technologies. ​

CON4 19. I can apply AI tools to improve teaching strategies. ​ CON5 20. I can adapt AI applications to suit cultural contexts in my teaching. ​

**Autonomy (AUT)** AUT1 21. I can decide when it is appropriate to use AI tools in my teaching and when not to. ​

AUT2 22. I am capable of learning new AI tools independently for teaching purposes. ​ AUT3 23. I can troubleshoot basic technical issues with AI tools used in the classroom. ​

AUT4 24. I am confident in guiding students on how to interact with AI responsibly. ​ AUT5 25. I feel prepared to design lessons without relying solely on AI, when necessary. ​

**Ethics (ETH)** ETH1 26. I actively consider students' privacy when using AI tools. Correlate ETH2 27. I prioritize ethical considerations when selecting AI tools for classroom use. Correlate ETH3 28. I can quickly identify ethical issues when using AI applications for my teaching. ​

ETH4 29. I can identify and address potential fairness issues when using AI for assessment. ​ ETH5 30. I feel responsible for ensuring that AI use in my teaching activities is ethical. ​
